list.listitem: Disorders and health habits that increase the uric acid pool (eg, obesity, alcohol use, meat consumption) increase a patient's risk of gout. B

A validated clinical decision rule can help rule in or rule out the diagnosis for many patients. C Algorithms including laboratory and imaging have good sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing gout. B

The definitive diagnosis is made by direct visualization of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals from joint aspirate or clinical criteria; clinical diagnosis and elevated serum uric acid is enough to make the diagnosis in many cases. C
There is no need to treat asymptomatic hyperuricemia. B
The acute treatment goal is relief of pain using NSAIDs, low-dose colchicine, or corticosteroids. B Electroacupuncture also appears useful as adjunctive treatment for pain relief. B

Treatment with allopurinol, as first-line urate-lowering therapy, is recommended in patients with a history of gout who have 2 or more gout flares annually, tophi, or joint damage on x-ray; urate-lowering therapy reduces long-term risk of acute gout flares.A Long-term use of febuxostat may increase risk of cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality. B

background.definition: Disease state resulting from deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints and tissues.

list.listitem: Annual incidence of gouty arthritis by serum urate (uric acid) level: At 9 mg/dL: 4.9% At 7 to 8.9 mg/dL: 0.5% Less than 7 mg/dL: 0.1%
For serum urate values greater than 9 mg/dL, the cumulative incidence of gout reaches 22% after 5 years.
In a cohort study of middle-aged adults, the cumulative incidence of gout by age 75 years is 11.8% for men and 5.0% for women.
Affects approximately 9.2 million US adults.
Male to female ratio ranges from 7:1 to 9:1.
Prevalence estimate using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data was 3.9% overall, 5.9% in men, and 2.0% in women.

The prevalence of gout in individuals with diabetes is higher at 16.7% (95% CI 15.1-18.3%; I2 = 99.30%); studies with small sample size, case-control design, and low quality score had higher prevalence rates than in well-designed, larger studies.

Approximately 55.8 million (95% uncertainty interval 44.4-69.8) people globally had gout in 2020, representing a 22.5% (20.9-24.2) increase since 1990 based on population-based data from 35 countries and claims data from the USA and Taiwan. The age-standardized prevalence was 659.3 (525.4-822.3) per 100,000.
Direct medical and prescription costs in the US were approximately $1800 per year higher for employees with gout.

Gout is associated with an increased risk of developing diabetes compared to patients with osteoarthritis (hazard ratio [HR] 1.5; 95% CI 1.45-1.54), especially in women. The relationship between gout and diabetes, however, may be due to comorbidities and not blood glucose.

Gout is also associated with a higher risk of atrial fibrillation (OR 1.4; 95% CI 1.3-1.6), deep vein thrombosis (HR 1.7; 95% CI 1.4-2.0), pulmonary embolus (HR 1.5; 95% CI 1.0-2.3), septic arthritis (multivariate HR 2.60; 95% CI 1.9-3.5),colorectal cancer (RR 1.22, 95% CI: 1.08-1.36), depression.

Among patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty, having gout increased the risk of postoperative complications including pulmonary embolism, wound complications and periprosthetic joint infection. There was an increased risk of early hip dislocation and need for revision.
Genetic predisposition.
Any systemic factor that increases uric acid levels (see Risk Factors).
Clinical manifestations are caused by urate crystal deposition in tissues with subsequent inflammation.
Hyperuricemia does not inevitably cause disease but does increase the likelihood.

Medications that can trigger a gouty flare include diuretics, low-dose salicylates, niacin, cyclosporine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Consider a change in these medications if patients experience a repeat gout attack.

Authors of a meta-analysis of cross-sectional data from 16 ,760 individuals of European ancestry concluded that foods associated with raised serum urate levels were alcohol (beer, liquor, wine), potato, poultry, soft drinks, and meat (beef, pork, or lamb) while foods associated with reduced serum urate levels were eggs, peanuts, cold cereal, skim milk, cheese, brown bread, margarine, and non-citrus fruits. These foods, however, explained little of the variation in serum urate levels.

Ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption was associated with a higher risk of gout with a hazard ratio of 1.16 (95% CI 1.01-1.33) comparing the lowest with the highest quartile of UPF consumption based on a prospective cohort study of 181,559 individuals from the UK Biobank study who were free of gout at baseline.

Normal uric acid levels in men and premenopausal women (7 and 6 mg/dL, respectively) are close to the limits of urate solubility. Solubility or urate at 37ºC is 6.8 mg/dL; above this level, urate begins to precipitate as crystals.

Crystals are phagocytosed by synoviocytes that release inflammatory factors. In a case-control study, individuals with acute and intercritical gout had increased circulating levels of the proinflammatory cytokine interleukin 8 (CXCL8) compared to healthy controls and disease-control patients.
Hyperuricemia in most patients (>90%) is due to reduced uric acid renal excretion; under 10% have uric acid overproduction.
There are 3 clinical stages of gout: acute phase (severe painful joint), intercritical (asymptomatic but disease progressing), and chronic tophaceous gout.
Limit alcohol consumption. A
Control obesity and hypertension; for the latter, with cautious use of diuretics. B
Lower meat and fish consumption and increase dairy products in diet. C
Avoid intravenous contrast dye because of the decreased glomerular filtration rate of uric acid. B

Among patients with gout and diabetes, initiation of a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor (canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, or empagliflozin) rather than dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors may reduce recurrent flares (52.4 and 79.7 events per 1000 person-years, respectively) and gout-primary ED visits and hospitalizations (0.5, 95% CI 0.3 to 0.8 and -3.4, 95% CI -5.8 to -0.9 per 1000 person-years, respectively) based on a population database.

For patients with asymptomatic hyperuricemia and chronic kidney disease, authors of a meta-analysis of 17 studies found treatment with uric-acid lowering therapy vs. placebo or no treatment preserved the loss of estimated glomerular filtration rate and reduced the increase in serum creatinine, although there was no difference in incidence rates of acute kidney injury.
Sudden onset of severe inflammatory arthritis in a peripheral joint with history of similar attacks separated by asymptomatic periods is suggestive. C
A clinical decision rule can determine the risk of gout based on the history, physical, and serum uric acid level.C
Direct visualization of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joint aspirate with polarized light microscopy is diagnostic when the diagnosis is uncertain. A
Serum uric acid may be useful in the context of a clinical rule, but should not be used alone to confirm or exclude the diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Fever, leukocytosis, elevated sedimentation rate; knee most commonly affected
Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate in aspirate; most common in knee, wrist, and shoulder
Symmetric joint involvement, usually hands; slow onset

list.listitem: Diagnostic criteria for gout are shown in .
Gout may also be diagnosed by either monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid or tophi confirmed with crystal examination.
The typical patient with acute gout presents with severe pain, redness, swelling, and disability of a single joint (80%-90%). Acute attacks can be polyarticular.

In a systematic review, women with gout were more likely than men to: be older, have hypertension or renal insufficiency, use diuretics, less likely to drink alcohol, have less frequent podagra but more often involvement of other joints, and have fewer recurrent attacks.
About 50% of initial attacks involve the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) (podagra). Ankle, wrist, knee, and olecranon bursae can also be involved.
Maximal pain is usually reached over several hours. An acute flare usually lasts 3 to 10 days without therapy.
Tophi deposits are common in the helix of ear, in the olecranon process, over interphalangeal joints, and in Heberden's or Bouchard's nodes.

The American College of Physicians (ACP) recommends treating for gout based on clinical findings and elevated serum uric acid, informed by a validated clinical decision rule. Joint aspiration can be considered to identify urate crystals under polarized light microscopy, or when septic joint is suspected. Crystals are needle-shaped and are strongly negatively birefringent under polarized light. Crystals are only found 85% of the time, but when present are very specific for gout.
Uric acid level (level normal in about 50% of gouty attacks).
Consider a 24-hour urine uric acid level, although there is poor patient adherence with the low-purine diet needed for an accurate test.

The delta neutrophil index, which represents the difference between leucocyte subfractions corresponding to the fraction of immature granulocytes, was useful in one study for differentiating between an acute gout attack and cellulitis; DNI was higher among those with cellulitis (2.8% vs. 0.6% for those with gout). The authors suggested a cut-off of greater than 1.7% to predict cellulitis.

For African American patients or patients of Asian descent who are under consideration for urate-lowering therapy, the American Collage of Rheumatology (ACR, 2020) conditionally recommends testing for the HLA-B*5801 allele which is associated with a markedly increased risk of allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome.
Radiographic findings may include asymmetric swelling and subcortical cysts without erosions. However, most patients do not have these findings, especially early in the course of the disease.
Ultrasound criteria are available for identifying gouty lesions, based on a Delphi technique.

In one study, three sonographic findings—the double contour sign, snowstorm appearance, and the presence of tophus—had modest accuracy in diagnosing gout if any 1 of the 3 was found, with a sensitivity of 77%, specificity of 84%, negative likelihood ratio 0.27, and positive likelihood ratio 4.9.

In a systematic review of diagnostic tests for gout for an American College of Physicians guideline, authors concluded that ultrasound had variable sensitivity (37%-100%) and high specificity (68%-97%) and that duel-energy computed tomography had good sensitivity and specificity (85%-100% and 83%-92%, respectively) for diagnosing gout based on low-quality evidence.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 28 studies examining dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) and ultrasound concluded that the pooled sensitivity and specificity of DECT were 0.89 (0.80-0.94) and 0.91 (0.88-0.94), respectively. The pooled sensitivity and specificity of US using double contour sign were 0.70 (0.58-0.79) and 0.95 (0.87-0.98), respectively; for tophus, 0.57 (0.38-0.74) and 0.99 (0.88-1.00), respectively; and for overall US, 0.84 (0.73-0.91) and 0.84 (0.78-0.89), respectively. Diagnostic sensitivity of DECT, however, is lower than overall US signs at disease duration <2 years.

The American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism 2015 classification criteria for gout were tested against the presence of MSU crystals in 381 patients presenting with monoarticular arthritis to Dutch physicians. Just over half (57%) were MSU-crystal positive. For the clinical-only version of the criteria, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.87 with a specificity of 84% and sensitivity of 68%, indicating good discriminative ability.
There are a number of algorithms including clinical, laboratory and imaging results that can be used to increase diagnostic certainty of gout. A validated clinical decision rule had good accuracy.
See algorithm in . Patients with a high likelihood of gout based on a validated clinical decision rule can be treated empirically.

When the diagnosis is in question, joint aspiration should be attempted to confirm the presence of MSU crystals. If unsuccessful or the patient refuses, a good response to a trial of colchicine supports the diagnosis.
Asymptomatic hyperuricemia rarely requires therapy. The 2020 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) guideline conditionally recommends against use of urate-lowering therapy in these patients. B
For an acute gout flare, treat with NSAIDs, low-dose colchicine or glucocorticoids (oral, intra-articular, or intramuscular). A
For monoarticular attacks, consider joint aspiration and corticosteroid injection. C

Urate-lowering therapy is recommended in patients with a history of gout who have frequent flares (2 or more annually), tophi, or joint damage on x-ray; the first-line agent is allopurinol. It is not recommended after an initial attack or in patients with infrequent attacks.A

Prophylactic colchicine at 0.6 mg twice daily, NSAIDs, or prednisone/prednisolone for 3-6 months is recommended per clinician discretion during initiation of antihyperuricemic therapy. A The 2017 American College of Physicians (ACP) guideline on treatment and prevention of acute gout recommends an overlap of at least 2 months of colchicine or an NSAID to prevent an early-treatment flare.
During an acute attack, if the patient is already on allopurinol do not stop it, and if the patient is not on allopurinol do not start it at that time. C

NSAIDs are considered first-line therapy followed by colchicine and/or corticosteroids or adrenocorticotropin hormone (ACTH); see . NSAIDs were similar with regards to pain reduction in acute gout to cyclooxygenase inhibitors (COXIBs) and glucocorticoids, but are associated with higher rates of adverse events compared with COXIBs. In general, it is important to start therapy as soon as possible to minimize pain, duration of attack, and disability. Do not use for long periods of time; most authors recommended a duration of treatment of 1 up to 2 weeks.

The ACP guideline recommends treatment with a corticosteroid, an NSAID (all equally effective), or low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg, followed by 0.6 mg after 1 hour); the guideline authors favor corticosteroid treatment given its high effectiveness, low cost, and low risk. The ACR 2020 guideline strongly recommends use of any of these 3 agents for an acute attack.

The British Society guideline recommends systemic or intra-articular anti-inflammatory agents, for monoarticular attacks, or colchicine for an acute attack. They also suggest use of rest, elevation and ice packs for acute attacks and full doses of NSAIDS or colchicine as first-line therapy, with the addition of gastroprotective medications when using NSAIDs or COXIBs (e.g. celecoxib). For patients with monoarticular attacks who have comorbidities, joint aspiration and corticosteroid injections may be the treatment of choice.

The European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) offers guidance on intra-articular therapies and recommends articular aspiration and injection of corticosteroids as one of the first-line treatments for an acute flare of gout; other suggested treatments include colchicine or oral corticosteroids.

Although uncommon, colchicine toxicity after acute ingestions exceeding 0.5 mg/kg has a high fatality rate; the lowest reported lethal dose of oral colchicine was 7 mg. Gastroenteritis-type symptoms begin 10 to 24 hours after ingestion followed by multiorgan dysfunction possibly resulting in death; recovery is usually complete and typically occurs within a few weeks of ingestion.

In one small RCT, low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg followed by 0.6 mg in 1 hour) was as effective as high-dose colchicine (1.2 mg followed by 0.6 mg every hour for 6 hours) for acute guot flares, with fewer adverse events (36% vs. 77%).
Oral prednisolone at 60 mg/d is as effective as naproxen for treatment of acute gout.

The British Society suggests consideration of interleukin (IL)-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab, or rilonacept) in patients who have not previously responded to standard treatment during acute attacks.

ACR 2020 guidelines conditionally recommend an IL-1 inhibitor over no therapy (beyond supportive/analgesic treatment) for patients experiencing a gout flare for whom anti-inflammatory therapies are either ineffective, poorly tolerated, or contraindicated.
Treatment with glucocorticoids (intramuscular, intravenous, or intraarticular) over IL-1 inhibitors or ACTH is strongly recommended by ACR 2020 for patients who are unable to take oral medications.

Authors of a network meta-analysis of RCTs found canakinumab, a human anti-interleukin-β monoclonal antibody, provided the highest pain reduction at day 2 compared to acetic acid-derivative NSAIDs and intravenous or intramuscular corticosteroids.

Begin urate-lowering therapy 2 weeks after attack if recurrent acute attacks, arthropathy, tophi, radiographic changes, or renal impairment (glomerular filtration rate <60) are present. The ACP and ACR 2020 guidelines recommend against beginning urate-lowering therapy after a first attack or in patients with infrequent attacks.

ACR 2020 guidelines conditionally recommend that if urate-lowering therapy will be needed, start treatment during the gout flare vs. starting urate-lowering therapy after the gout flare has resolved. The British Society of Rheumatology guideline, however, suggests waiting until inflammation has resolved. Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs including 479 patients found longer days to resolution (standard mean difference 0.3, 95% CI 0.1–0.6), but similar rates of pain on visual analog scale and rate of recurrent gout attacks by 30 days comparing initiation of urate-lowering therapy during an acute gout episode vs. controls.
Allopurinol decreases urate synthesis and probenecid increases urinary loss of uric acid ().

Pain outcomes at day 3 do not appear different for people starting urate-lowering therapy during an acute attack compared with those who do not. Interestingly, in this meta-analysis, there was no substantial difference in the recurrence rate of acute gout attacks based on use of allopurinol (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.19; I2 0%). Other authors demonstrated no increase in flare duration if starting urate-lowering treatment.

For patients starting urate-lowering therapy, prophylactic use of colchicine or NSAIDs for at least 8 weeks reduces the risk of acute gout attacks by at least half. ACR 2020 strongly recommends administering concomitant anti-inflammatory prophylaxis therapy (eg, colchicine, NSAIDs, prednisone/ prednisolone).

Consider prophylactic treatment with NSAIDs (6 weeks recommended) or colchicine (0.6 mg every other day up to twice daily) to minimize the risk of acute flare from uric acid mobilization from tophi. Stop colchicine 3 to 6 months after normouricemia or tophaceous lesions disappear. One study showed that 64% of patients had an acute flare in the first year of allopurinol therapy.

In a recent study, for every 100 people treated with combined allopurinol with colchicine, they were twice as likely to have diarrhea (8 people) compared to those with allopurinol alone (3 to 4 people) as well as slightly higher risk of myocardial infarction (1 extra), neuropathy (1 extra), and muscle pain (less than 1 extra). For every 100 people treated with combined allopurinol with NSAIDs, there was greater risk of angina (4 to 5 people) than those who took allopurinol alone (3 to 4 people) as well as a slightly increased risk of myocardial infarction and kidney damage (less than 1 extra).
Consider switching to an alternative agent in patients who take hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension.
For those with comorbid diabetes mellitus, consider adding or switching to SGLT2i for lower rates of recurrent flares of gout when compared to sulfonylureas.

ACR 2020 guidelines recommend treatment with allopurinol for most patients with a history of gout who have 2 or more gout flares annually, tophi, or joint damage on x-ray. Treatment can be considered in patients with fewer attacks. Either allopurinol or febuxostat is strongly recommended for patients with moderate-to-severe chronic kidney disease.

The ACP guideline recommends allopurinol or febuxostat as first-line uricosuric agents based on strong evidence that these agents lower serum uric acid levels and moderate evidence that they reduce the frequency of gouty attacks. However, there are safety concerns regarding increased cardiovascular and all-cause mortality with febuxostat.
Starting treatment with low-dose allopurinol (≤100 mg/day and lower in patients with CKD [stage ≥3]) or febuxostat (≤40 mg/day) with subsequent dose titration is strongly recommended by ACR 2020.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 RCTs including 7968 patients with hyperuricemic gout concluded that all urate-lowering therapies (ULTs) were effective in achieving the target serum urate level at 6 months compared with placebo. Febuxostat was superior to allopurinol and well tolerated. Lesinurad in combination with febuxostat or allopurinol was effective in urate lowering, but appears to have a high risk of AEs

In a single-institution Chinese cohort study including 582 male patients with gout seen as outpatients, compared to colchicine prophylaxis, initiation of low-dose febuxostat (20 mg daily) alone was not associated with an increased risk of gout flares during the 6-week follow up (HR) 1.3, 95% CI 0.6-2.7), but use of initial high-dose febuxostat at 40 mg daily was associated with an increased risk of gout flares (HR 3.1, 95% CI 1.3-7.1).

Treating to a uric acid level of less than 6 mg/dL has been shown to decrease gout attacks, and ACR recommends treating to this target level. Slow uric acid lowering using 0.6 mg/dL per month is best. The ACP 2017 guidelines note that there is no need for a 24-hour urine monitoring or ongoing uric acid monitoring; just use standard doses of allopurinol or febuxostat. The British Society guideline continues to recommend treatment to target uric acid levels. Medications used in an acute painful flare are not good at reducing urate levels. Conversely, urate-lowering medications are ineffective as painkillers and should not be started or stopped during an acute flare.

Febuxostat, a nonpurine-based oral xanthine oxidase inhibitor, is likely comparable to allopurinol in effectiveness. In one RCT with 314 subjects with hyperuricemia and early gout, febuxostat vs. placebo significantly reduced the incidence of gout flares (29.3% versus 41.4%) and improved serum uric acid control (62.8% versus 5.7%). Febuxostat is cleared through liver and so can be used in patients with renal disease. Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs found that use of febuxostat improved estimated glomerular filtration rate in patients with gout and chronic kidney disease.

However, there are concerns about safety, adverse effects, and cost of febuxostat. In a RCT of 6190 patients with known cardiovascular disease and gout, of whom 656 subjects remained in the trial, higher cardiovascular (CV) and all-cause mortality was found at 5 years in the febuxostat vs. allopurinol group (4.3% vs. 3.2% for CV mortality and 7.8% vs. 6.4% for all cause-mortality, respectively). Authors of a meta-analysis of cardiovascular outcomes in patients with gout but not known cardiovascular disease found no decrease or increase in cardiovascular outcomes in the short term and no significant difference between febuxostat and allopurinol (40/3631 vs. 5/1154, respectively; RR 1.69, 95% CI 0.54-5.34). In the 4 longer-term RCTs, there was a trend towards increased cardiovascular events in the febuxostat group but not all-cause mortality.

In a recent cohort study of 976 patients with advanced kidey disease treated with febuxostat or allopurinol, febuxostat was associated with lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.64-0.98) and fewer hospitalizations (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.44-0.63) compared to allopurinol and febuxostat reduced hospitalizations for heart failure (HR 0.59, 95% CI 0.44-0.80) and infection (HR 0.65, 95% CI 0.52-0.82).

Based on an international position paper, the British Society of Rheumatology, and a NICE guideline, febuxostat should not be considered a first-line agent but would be appropriate to prescribe for patients who have failed or are intolerant to allopurinol. Data are lacking on use of febuxostat in allopurinol allergy. Information is available on contraindications and monitoring in the report.

In patients who are resistant or intolerant to xanthine oxidase inhibitors, use a uricosuric agent such as sulfinpyrazone or probenecid. If starting probenecid, ACR 2020 guidelines conditionally recommend starting with a low-dose (500 mg once to twice daily) with subsequent dose titration over starting at a higher dose.

Lesinurad, a selective uric acid reabsorption inhibitor that also increases uric acid excretion, was tested as monotherapy and found to be more effective than placebo in 214 total patients unable to take xanthine oxidase inhibitors (29.9% vs. 1.9% achieved uric acid levels of 6 mg/dl or lower), but the trial was discontinued early due primarily to renal serious adverse events (4.7%) and serum creatinine elevations of 1.5 times baseline (24.3%).

Canakinumab is also under investigation for the treatment of acute and chronic gouty arthritis. Other drugs under investigation are uricosuric agents verinurad and arhalofenate (also an anti-inflammatory drug), and the xanthine oxidase inhibitor topiroxostat which was found to be superior to placebo in reaching target serum uric acid level, and non-inferior to allopurinol for uric acid reduction in a Japanese RCT.

Pegloticase is a newer FDA-approved drug for refractory gout, based on 2 small 6-month trials. It is given IV every 2 to 4 weeks. In one RCT, both every 2 week and monthly pegloticase significantly improved global disease assessment, disability and physical domains of the short-form 36; pain was also reduced using the biweekly regimen. The drug’s effectiveness is limited by the development of antibodies. ACR 2020 guideline strongly recommends against its use as a first-line agent.

A monthly proprietary infusion of rapamycin-containing nanoparticle and pegadricase looks promising for treatment of refractory gout with similar efficacy and tolerability comparable to pegloticase. In this phase 2 RCT of patients with refractory gout, monthly sequential infusions of a proprietary rapamycin-containing nanoparticle (ImmTOR) and pegadricase compared to twice monthly infusions of pegloticase resulted in greater reductions in serum urate level at 3 and 6 months with similar reductions in gout flare incidence and number of tender and/or swollen joints. Side effect rates of infection and infusion reactions were similar with the exception of stomatitis (9.6%) associated with ImmTOR only.

In an RCT of adjunctive lesinurad in 603 patients taking allopurinol who were not at target uric acid levels, those randomized to the addition of lesinurad at either 200 mg or 400 mg were more likely that those on allopurinol and placebo to reach target uric acid levels at 6 months (54.2%, 59.2%, and 27.9%, respectively), but there were no differences in flares or resolution of tophi. Higher incidences of predominantly reversible elevations of serum creatinine level were seen in the lesinurad groups. In another RCT of 324 patients taking febuxostat who were not at target uric acid level and had at least 1 tophus, patients randomized to the addition of 400 mg lesinurad vs. 200 mg or placebo were more likely to achieve target uric acid level (75.1% vs. 56.6% and 46.8%, respectively), although more patients in this group had higher rates of predominantly reversible elevations of serum creatinine level.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that pegloticase is probably effective for resolution of tophi. It also concluded that lesinurad 400 mg + febuxostat is more effective than lesinurad 200 mg + febuxostat, but comparisons with placebo were not found. Lesinurad + allopurinol was probably not effective for resolution of tophi.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs found that lesinurad 200 mg + Xanthine oxidase inhibitor (XOI) and lesinurad 400 mg + XOI lowered serum uric acid levels to a greater degree than the XOI alone. However, with the higher dose of lesinurad (400 mg), there was an increase in treatment-emergent adverse events.
Losartan, vitamin C, and fenofibrate have uricosuric properties and may be useful adjuncts for patients with gout, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.

strong.em: Switching therapy for persistent hyperuricemia or unresolved tophi

list.listitem: ACR 2020 guidelines conditionally recommend switching to a second xanthine oxidase inhibitor over adding a uricosuric agent for patients taking their first drug who have persistently high serum urate concentrations (>6 mg/dl) despite maximum-tolerated or FDA-indicated dose, and who have continued frequent gout flares (>2 flares/year) OR non-resolving subcutaneous tophi.

ACR 2020 strongly recommends switching to pegloticase over continuing current urate-lowering therapy for patients with gout for whom xanthine oxidase inhibitor treatment, uricosurics, and other interventions have failed to achieve the serum urate target, and who continue to have frequent gout flares (≥2 flares/year) OR who have non-resolving subcutaneous tophi. This switch is recommended against if patients have infrequent gout flares and no tophi.

Surgery may be needed to treat complications of tophaceous disease: infection (eg, incision and drainage), compression because of the mass effect of tophus (eg, excision, surgical decompression), joint deformity (eg, joint replacement), and intractable pain (eg, excision).

In one case series of 16 patients, ankle replacement resulted in good outcomes at 5 years with respect to pain and SF-36 scores; one patient required revision at 4.7 years for painful prosthetic loosening.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 27 RCTs with 1951 patients concluded that external-use herbal medicines appear to be safe and effective for treatment of pain and symptoms of acute gouty arthritis compared to western medicine control groups.

In a 12-week RCT of 210 patients with gout, the 114/139 randomized to plant-based tufuling oral liquid who remained on treatment vs. 59/71 who remained on placebo had fewer flares (21.9% and 50.9%, respectively); there were no serious adverse events in either group.

Acupuncture appears to reduce uric acid levels, although data are conflicting regarding benefit compared to Western medicine. In 4 of the 10 trials in this meta-analysis, acupuncture was slightly better than Western therapy in decreasing pain scores, but the difference was not clinically important. No data were provided on gouty attacks.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 Chinese RCTs including 1076 patients found electroacupuncture as an adjunct to treatment reduced uric acid levels and pain better than conventional Western drug treatment alone (MD -31.6, 95% CI -44.2 to -19 and MD -2.3, 95% CI -2.7 to -1.8, respectively). Although the authors found low to moderate risk of bias by the Cochrane risk of bias tool, no sham treatment arms were included and blinding was not feasible resulting in high risk of performance bias.
Local ice therapy may reduce pain and inflammation. ACR 2020 gives topical ice a conditional recommendation.

Educate patients with gout about management of acute attacks, optimal diet (low-fat, eliminate purine-rich foods), avoiding alcohol, reducing obesity, and disease management strategies; urate-lowering therapy can be continued during attacks. Nurse led post hospitalization appointments with focus on patient education and awareness of urate-lowering therapy led to increased utilization of urate-lowering therapy and achieving urate target level.

In a British non-blinded RCT of 517 adult patients who had experienced a gout flare in the previous 12 months, patients randomized to a nurse-led intervention vs. usual care were more likely to have serum urate concentrations less than the target of 6 mg/dL (95% vs 30%, RR 3.18, 95% CI 2.42-4.18), fewer gout flares (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.19-0.57) and lower risk of having any tophi (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.08-–0.52) at 2 years. The nurse intervention consisted of individualized education and frequent face-to-face (mean visits 9.34) or telephone contact (mean calls 8.33); most contacts occurred during the first year of the trial. Cost per quality-adjusted life-year gained for the nurse intervention at 2 years was £5066.

Evidence supporting lifestyle change strategies comes from observational studies. In the single RCT reviewed by Cochrane authors, skimmed milk powder enriched with glycomacropeptide and G600 did not reduce the frequency of gouty attacks compared to standard skim milk or lactose powder, although the frequency of attacks decreased in all 3 groups.

In a small RCT including 103 patients with prehypertension or stage I hypertension, those following the Dietary Approach to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet reduced their uric acid levels in one study by -0.35 mg/dl (95% CI -0.65 to -0.05); the decrease was more pronounced in those with elevated uric acid.

EULAR 2021 guideline for inflammatory arthritis includes implementation strategies for self-management, self-efficacy, and patient organizations to empower individuals with gout to participate in their care for improved outcomes (expert opinion).
Patients with urolithiasis should consume at least 2 liters of water daily, avoid dehydration, and take potassium citrate (60 mEq daily) (expert opinion).

Vitamin C at doses of 500 mg daily has been shown to reduce serum uric acid levels by 0.5 mg/dL. In one small RCT, however, the addition of 500 mg of vitamin C for patients already taking allopurinol and not at target level decreased uric acid only negligibly (0.2 mg/dL). The potential effect of vitamin C on gouty attacks was not assessed.
Cherries at 0.5 lb per day for 2 weeks, cherry juice, or tablets may reduce uric acid levels, as may folic acid at 10 to 75 mg/d, which inhibits xanthine oxidase.
However, clinical trials demonstrating reduced flares or other improved clinical outcomes for these interventions are lacking.
Lower levels of serum urate during treatment correlate with a longer delay before acute attacks resume or tophi reappear.

ACR 2020 guidelines conditionally recommend continuing urate-lowering therapy indefinitely. Patients with serum levels less than 5.05 mg/dL during continuous treatment of at least 6 years have an 80% relapse rate within 5 years of stopping antihyperuricemic agents.
The majority of patients with long-term antihyperuricemic therapy will have recurrent symptoms, tophi, or both if treatment is stopped.
Uric acid mobilization from tophi can cause an acute flare. Consider prophylactic colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily or NSAIDs.
Silent bony erosions and tophaceous deposits are not prevented by colchicine or NSAIDs; use uric acid-lowering medications.
Long-term colchicine is associated with renal dysfunction; monitor renal function. Contraindicated in patients on dialysis. Side effects decrease with once daily or every other day dosing.

Rarely, allopurinol can cause fatal hypersensitivity syndrome (rash, fever, eosinophilia, and hepatitis) with a mortality rate of 20%; monitor and discontinue if symptoms develop. HLA-B*58:01 genotyping can help predict patients at risk of hypersensitivity but authors of a decision analysis concluded that number needed to test to prevent one case of adverse drug reaction was 11,286 (95% central range 2573 to 53,594) rendering this approach not currently cost-effective. As noted above, ACR conditionally recommends testing for the HLA-B*5801 allele in African Americans and patients of Asian descent prior to initiating treatment for gout.

In a population-based study in Taiwan, the annual incidence rate of a hypersensitivity reaction among new users of allopurinol was approximately 1 in 200; risk was higher in patients treated for asymptomatic hyperuricemia and among those with renal or cardiovascular disease.
Probenecid is associated with a risk of uric acid urinary stones; prevent with good hydration.
The British Society guidelines recommend that patients with urolithiasis consume at least 2 liters of water daily, avoid dehydration, and take potassium citrate (60 mEq daily).
Tophaceous deposits may rarely compress peripheral nerves, the cauda equina, or the spinal cord. Prompt surgical decompression is essential to prevent permanent neurologic impairment.
Prognosis is good with significant patient adherence and correct prescribing. C
About 60% of patients who experience an acute gouty attack will have another attack within 12 months. B
In patients with a history of gout, higher serum urate levels at baseline are associated with an increasing risk of subsequent gout flares and rates of hospitalizations for recurrent gout. B
Natural history of acute flare without treatment is 3 to 10 days.
With each succeeding attack, the intercritical (clinically silent) period grows shorter, and the flares become longer and more severe.
Untreated tophaceous gout can cause joint erosion and destruction.
About 60% of patients who experience a gouty attack will have another attack within 12 months.
There is no need to treat asymptomatic hyperuricemia unless there is a strong family history of tophaceous disease or gout.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 studies with 7757 patients concluded that urate-lowering therapy was not associated with a reduction in CVD events; most studies, however, were less than one-year duration.
In addition, there is no association between all-cause mortality and allopurinol use in patients with gout compared to patients with gout not using allopurinol.
Acute flares are rare if uric acid level are less than 6 mg/dL.

The Rheumatic Diseases Comorbidity Index (RDCI) and gout-specifically modified RDCI are highly correlated with each other as well as with the Charlson Comorbidity Index and the Functional Comorbidity Index and moderately to weakly associated with health outcomes such as physical functioning and physical health.

Baseline serum urate levels are associated with recurrent gout in a graded manner: rates of acute gout flares per 1000 person-years are 10.6 for urate levels less than 6 mg/dL, 40.1 for levels of 6.0 to 6.9 mg/dL, 82 for levels of 7.0 to 7.9 mg/dL, 101.3 for levels of 8.0 to 8.9 mg/dL, 125.3 for levels of 9.0 to 9.9 mg/dL, and 132.8 for levels greater than or equal to 10 mg/dL.

Gout flares are also related to co-morbidities. In a one-year follow-up study of 2639 patients sorted into 5 clusters by type of co-morbidities, those (n=437) with the highest proportion of cardiovascular disease (53%), chronic kidney disease (56%), and cancer (7%) had the highest incidence (71.9%) and earliest onset (median 3 months) of gout flares. In contrast, those with obesity (n=258) had the lowest incidence (52.1%) and the latest onset (median 10 months) of gout flares. Age at diagnosis of gout, duration of gout, presence of tophi, and smoking ≥ 20 cigarettes/day were also associated with gout flares.

The ACP no longer recommends checking uric acid levels in patients on standard doses of allopurinol or febuxostat. The British Society guideline continues to recommend treatment to target uric acid levels (initially to <5 mg/dL and later to <6 mg/dL).
Monitor for symptoms of allopurinol-related rash and/or fever.
Gout in pregnancy is very rare.
NSAIDs and colchicine are unsafe in pregnancy.
Allopurinol is pregnancy category C, and probenecid is pregnancy category B.
Disease not routinely seen unless there is a genetic metabolic problem.

cell.label: Patient presents with intensely painful, swollen joint in typical location. Past similar episodes. Gout likely using clinical decision rule?
Diagnosis in question; attempt joint aspiration. Positive gram stain and/or culture?
Patient refuses aspiration or unsuccessful in obtaining fluid. Consider colchicine trial for 1-2 d and assess response.
Obtain serum uric acid and, if elevated, treat with urate-lowering therapy.
Treat empirically with NSAIDs, steroids, or colchicine. Episode resolves?

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Gout.
feature.feature_body: Diagnosis of gout can be made clinically with the presence of at least 6 of these 12 features: Recurrent arthritic attack Maximal inflammation develops within 24 h Monarticular arthritis Joint redness Pain or swelling in the first MTP joint Unilateral attack involving first MTP Unilateral attack involving tarsal joint Suspected tophus Hyperuricemia Asymmetric swelling within a joint (radiograph) Subcortical cysts without erosions (radiograph) Negative culture of joint fluid Data from Wallace SL, Robinson H, Masi AT, Decker JL, McCarty DJ, Yu TF. Preliminary criteria for the classification of the acute arthritis of primary gout. Arthritis Rheum 1977;20:895–900.

Start 250 mg twice daily; maintenance therapy 500-1000 mg 2-3 times daily. If urinary uric acid level over 700 mg, best to use allopurinol to avoid ureteral stones. Contraindicated in patients with past nephrolithiasis and CrCl <50 mL/min.
Starting dose is 40 mg daily. If serum uric acid level below 6 not achieved in 2 weeks, increase to 80mg. No adjustment necessary for mild to moderate renal impairment.
Not available in U.S. Starting dose is 25 mg per day. Usual effective dose is 100mg per day with maximum of 200 mg per day. Relative contraindication in patients at risk for nephrolithiasis.

Not available in U.S. Begin with 50 mg twice per day. Usual effective dose is 100-200 mg three to four times per day. Ineffective with GFR less than 60 mL/min. Relative contraindication in patients at risk for nephrolithiasis.
